items.short: The coffee species behind most specialty coffee — sweeter, more aromatic, and more delicate to grow.
items.deep: Arabica accounts for roughly 60% of world coffee. It thrives at higher, cooler elevations, which slows the cherry’s growth and builds sugars and acidity. That nuance is also why it’s fussier: more vulnerable to heat, pests, and disease than robusta.
items.example: A bag that says “100% Arabica” is signalling a softer, more flavour-forward cup.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: Compared with robusta, arabica usually has…
check.explain: Arabica is prized for sweetness and bright acidity; robusta carries more caffeine and bitterness.

items.short: A tougher coffee species with nearly double the caffeine — bolder, more bitter, and easier to farm.
items.deep: Coffea canephora (robusta) grows well at low elevations in hot, humid climates and resists disease, so it’s cheaper to produce. It brings heavy body and a grain-like bitterness, and shows up in espresso blends for crema and punch, and in instant coffee.
items.example: A little robusta in an espresso blend can deepen the crema and add a caffeine kick.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: Robusta is best known for…

choices.t: About twice the caffeine of arabica

check.explain: Robusta carries ~2.4% caffeine vs arabica’s ~1.2%, and grows happily at low elevation.

items.short: A cultivated variety of coffee plant, bred or selected for traits like flavour, yield, or disease resistance.
items.deep: Think of cultivars the way you think of apple varieties — Bourbon, Typica, Geisha and SL28 are all arabica, but each brings its own character. Some are chosen for cup quality, others for surviving leaf rust.
items.example: “Geisha” on a label points to a prized cultivar famous for jasmine-like aromatics.

check.q: A cultivar is best described as…

choices.t: A cultivated variety of the coffee plant

check.explain: A cultivar is a specific cultivated variety — like Bourbon or Geisha.

items.short: One of the two ancestral arabica varieties — the line most coffee outside Africa descends from.
items.deep: Typica travelled out of Yemen and through Java and the Caribbean, seeding plantations across Latin America and Asia. It gives a clean, sweet, elegant cup but yields poorly and catches disease easily, so most farms now grow its descendants rather than Typica itself.
items.example: Jamaica Blue Mountain and old Hawaiian Kona plantings are Typica.

items.short: The other ancestral arabica variety — sweeter and higher-yielding than Typica, and the parent of Caturra and Catuaí.
items.deep: Named for the island of Bourbon (now Réunion), where it was planted separately from the Typica line. It carries more sugar and a rounder body, and mutated into much of what Latin America grows today. Red, yellow, orange and pink Bourbons differ in cherry colour, not in ancestry.
items.example: A bag reading “Red Bourbon” is naming this variety, not a whiskey barrel.

check.q: Bourbon and Typica are…
check.explain: Almost every arabica grown today descends from one of these two lines.

items.short: A natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon — shorter plants, easier picking, widely grown across Latin America.
items.deep: Discovered in Brazil in the early 20th century. Its compact height lets farms plant densely and harvest without ladders, and it keeps much of Bourbon’s sweetness — which is why it spread so fast through Colombia and Central America.
items.example: Most Colombian and Costa Rican lots are Caturra or one of its offspring.

items.short: A famously floral, tea-like variety — the most expensive coffee on most shelves, and a fussy, low-yielding plant.
items.deep: Collected in Ethiopia, held in collections for decades, then made famous when a Panamanian farm won a 2004 competition with it. At the right altitude it gives jasmine and bergamot aromatics unlike anything else; grown too low it is unremarkable. The plant yields little, so the price is real rather than pure hype.
items.example: A bag reading “Geisha” costs several times a neighbouring lot from the same farm.

check.q: Geisha is best known for…

choices.t: Floral, tea-like aromatics at a high price

check.explain: It is prized for jasmine-like florals — and it yields poorly, which is why it costs what it does.

items.short: A Kenyan variety selected in the 1930s, behind the blackcurrant acidity Kenyan coffee is known for.
items.deep: The “SL” is Scott Laboratories, the Nairobi station that selected it — SL28 and SL34 were the two that stuck. SL28 is drought-tolerant and deep-rooted but vulnerable to leaf rust, and it is grown almost entirely in Kenya, which is why the flavour reads as a country signature.
items.example: A Nyeri lot listing SL28 is the classic Kenyan profile.

items.short: A catch-all for Ethiopia’s thousands of wild and local arabica types, where no single variety name is recorded.
items.deep: Ethiopia is arabica’s birthplace, and its coffee grows as mixed local populations rather than named, catalogued varieties. “Heirloom” on a bag is honest but vague — it tells you the coffee is Ethiopian and genetically diverse, not what to expect in the cup. Region and processing are the more useful lines on that bag.
items.example: “Yirgacheffe, heirloom, washed” — the region and process carry the information.

items.short: The fruit of the coffee plant. Each cherry usually holds two seeds — the “beans” we roast.
items.deep: A coffee bean is a seed, and the cherry is the fruit it grew in: skin, sweet pulp, sticky mucilage, then two seeds pressed flat against each other. Sugar builds up in the fruit while it hangs on the branch, and nobody further down the chain can add it later — so an unripe cherry gives the mill and the roaster nothing to work with. It takes about five to six kilos of cherry to make one kilo of green coffee.
items.example: A branch ripens unevenly, which is why hand-picked lots get walked several times in a season.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: A picker strips a branch, ripe and unripe cherries together. What does that cost the lot?

choices.t: Nothing much; roasting evens ripeness out
Caffeine, which forms only as fruit ripens

check.explain: Ripeness is decided on the branch. The mill can sort out the worst cherries and the roaster can do a careful job, but neither one adds sugar that was never there. The caffeine is in the seed either way, so what you lose is sweetness, not strength.

items.short: A single round seed from a cherry that grew only one — sorted into its own lot, and priced as if that were a grade.
items.deep: A cherry normally sets two seeds that flatten against each other. When only one of the two ovules is fertilised, the lone seed grows with nothing to press it flat, so it comes out small, round and dense. It happens in roughly 5% of cherries, on the same branches as everything else — it is not a variety, and nobody can plant it. Mills sieve peaberries out because round, dense beans move and take heat differently in a roaster, which is a real reason to keep them apart and a poor reason to expect a better cup.
items.example: “Tanzania Peaberry” names the shape of the bean in the bag, not a cupping score.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee
Perfect Daily Grind — What Are Peaberry Coffee Beans?

check.q: A peaberry forms when…

choices.t: Only one of the cherry’s two seeds is fertilised
A farmer plants the peaberry variety
A bean cracks in half during roasting

check.explain: One seed, nothing to flatten it, so it grows round. It is chance inside an ordinary cherry — which is why a peaberry lot has to be sieved out rather than grown.

items.short: The band around the equator, roughly 25°N to 25°S, where coffee grows best.
items.deep: Coffee needs a narrow climate: arabica likes an average of about 18–22 °C and no frost at all. Those conditions sit either side of the equator. Height and latitude are two ways to reach them — farms on the equator climb high for cool nights, while farms near the edges of the belt find the same temperatures much lower down. A warming climate is pushing that window uphill, which is one reason altitude now appears on so many bags.
items.example: Kenyan farms on the equator sit near 1,700 m; Brazilian ones at 20°S grow well below 1,200 m.

sources.label: Foods (MDPI) — Does Coffee Have Terroir and How Should It Be Assessed?

check.q: Why do Kenyan farms sit so much higher than Brazilian ones?

choices.t: Altitude supplies the cool it needs
Kenyan soil is only fertile high up
Arabica needs thin air to ripen properly

check.explain: Height and distance from the equator both get you to the same cool temperatures. It is also why “high grown” means different numbers in different countries.

items.short: The sense of place in a cup — how soil, altitude and climate shape a coffee’s flavour.
items.deep: Terroir is the whole growing environment turning up in the cup: altitude, soil, rainfall, shade, and how far the temperature drops overnight. Cooler, higher farms ripen their cherries slowly, and slow ripening is the usual explanation for denser beans with more acidity and more going on. Coffee has no legal definition of terroir the way wine does — and a heavy roast or a bold processing style will drown it out.
items.example: Two farms on one Colombian slope, 300 m apart in height, cup differently every harvest.

sources.label: Foods (MDPI) — Does Coffee Have Terroir and How Should It Be Assessed?

check.q: A roaster says a coffee “tastes of its terroir”. What has to hold steady for that to mean anything?

choices.t: The variety, since terroir is really genetics

check.explain: Terroir is a claim about a place, so everything that happens after the farm has to stay the same before you can taste it. Variety is a separate thing: that is genetics, not ground.

items.short: Metres above sea level — a shorthand some bags print instead of writing out the growing altitude.
items.deep: Nothing more than a unit label: “1,900 masl” means grown at 1,900 metres. It is trade shorthand rather than something you need to say out loud, and plenty of bags skip it and print “1,900 m” or feet instead. What matters is the number, and that there is one at all — a specific altitude is a quality signal, no altitude tells you nothing.
items.example: “1,900 masl” and “grown at 1,900 metres” mean exactly the same thing.

items.short: The sticky, sugary gel glued to the coffee seed under the fruit — the layer processing is really about.
items.deep: Mucilage sits between the pulp and the parchment and won’t rinse off with water alone: it either ferments loose or dries onto the seed. How much of it stays on while the coffee dries is the whole difference between washed, honey and natural.
items.example: Leave the mucilage on and its sugars ferment into berry and body; rinse it off and the cup turns clean and bright.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: Mucilage is…

choices.t: The papery shell around the seed
A sugary gel stuck to the seed

check.explain: It’s the honey-like gel between fruit and parchment — and how much stays on decides washed, honey or natural.

items.short: The papery shell around a coffee seed. Coffee rests and ships inside it, then is hulled before export.
items.deep: Once the fruit and mucilage are gone, the seed is still wrapped in this dry husk, which protects it during storage. Hulling — removing the parchment — usually happens as late as possible, just before the coffee leaves for the roaster.
items.example: A lot sold “in parchment” hasn’t been hulled yet — it’s still wearing layer 04.

items.short: The tissue-thin membrane on a green bean. Most of it lifts off in the roaster as chaff.
items.deep: Silverskin is the last layer between parchment and seed. Roasting dries it and it flakes away as chaff, which roasters collect and discard — except in the centre crease, where a little usually stays behind. On naturals that trapped silverskin often looks stained.
items.example: Those papery flakes in the bottom of a home roaster are silverskin, not burnt coffee.

items.short: The S-shaped crease down the flat face of a bean, where it was pressed against its twin inside the cherry.
items.deep: The centre cut is the first thing graders look at. It traps leftover silverskin, so it also records how the coffee was processed: pale and clean on a washed lot, often stained amber or reddish on a natural where fruit sugar dried in place.
items.example: Tip beans onto a white plate and read the crease — pale usually means washed, stained usually means natural.

items.short: The natural stimulant in coffee — around 95 mg in a mug of drip, and far less in a single espresso.
items.deep: Caffeine is the plant’s built-in pesticide, and how much lands in your cup depends on species, brew and serving size. Robusta carries roughly twice arabica’s share, and a long steep plus a big glass is why cold brew often tops the chart while a small espresso sits well below a mug of drip.
items.example: A 30 ml espresso (~63 mg) delivers less caffeine than a 240 ml mug of drip (~95 mg).

check.q: Which usually delivers the most caffeine per serving?
check.explain: Cold brew’s long steep and large serving add up — often ~200 mg, double a mug of drip.

items.short: The fruit is stripped and the seeds are fermented and rinsed clean before drying — giving a clean, bright cup.
items.deep: Also called the “wet” process. Removing the fruit early lets the bean’s own character and acidity shine, with less of the fruit’s influence. It needs plenty of water and careful fermentation control.
items.example: Washed Kenyans are famous for their crisp, almost blackcurrant-like acidity.

check.q: Washed coffees tend to taste…

choices.t: Heavier and sweeter than a natural

check.explain: Removing the fruit early gives washed coffees their signature clarity and acidity.

items.short: The whole cherry is dried with the fruit still on, pushing fruity, sometimes wine-like sweetness into the bean.
items.deep: The oldest method: cherries dry in the sun for weeks before the dried fruit is removed. It uses little water but demands constant turning to avoid mould. Results are heavier-bodied and fruit-forward.
items.example: A natural Ethiopian can taste of blueberry and ripe strawberry.

check.q: In the natural process, the cherry is…
check.explain: Naturals dry with the fruit attached, which is where the bold fruity sweetness comes from.

items.short: A middle path: some fruit pulp is left on the bean during drying, balancing sweetness and clarity.
items.deep: The skin and some pulp are removed, but the sticky layer underneath — the mucilage — is left on the seed while it dries. There is no honey in it; the name describes how the wet seed feels. Producers grade the result by colour: yellow honey dries fastest and cleanest, red takes longer, black is slowest and sweetest. More mucilage left on means more sugar fermenting in place, and more risk of mould if the beds are not turned often enough.
items.example: “Black honey” means most of the mucilage stayed on through a long, shaded dry.

sources.label: Barista Magazine — Understanding the Process: Honey

check.q: A bag says “red honey”. What are you being told?

choices.t: That honey was added during processing
That the coffee was roasted medium-dark

check.explain: Honey grades describe how much mucilage was left on and how slowly it dried. Nothing is added, and it says nothing about the roast. Washed and natural sit at the two ends of that same dial.

items.short: The controlled breakdown of the cherry’s sugars that develops flavour during processing.
items.deep: Every coffee ferments — microbes eat the sticky, sugary mucilage off the seed whether the method is washed, natural or honey. What producers control is time, temperature and oxygen: careful, short ferments keep a cup clean; long or sealed ones push it fruity, winey, even boozy.
items.example: An “anaerobic natural” on a label means the cherries fermented in a sealed tank — expect loud, winey fruit.

check.q: During fermentation, the microbes are eating…

choices.t: The sugary mucilage around the seed

check.explain: Microbes strip the sticky fruit layer off the seed — that work, and its byproducts, shape the flavour.

items.short: Fermenting cherries in sealed, oxygen-free tanks — slower microbes, louder and funkier flavours.
items.deep: Cherries or depulped seeds ferment in sealed tanks. With the oxygen gone the usual microbes cannot work, CO₂ builds up, and a different set of yeasts and bacteria takes over. Because the producer sets the time and temperature instead of leaving it to the weather, the loud, wine-like flavours come out the same way batch after batch. It is the newest style on most shelves, and the easiest to push too far.
items.example: A sealed ferment of several days before drying is what puts “cinnamon, plum” on a competition bag.

sources.label: PMC — Effect of processing method (natural, washed, honey, fermentation, maceration) on specialty coffee

check.q: What does sealing the tank actually change?

choices.t: The temperature, which drives all fermentation
Nothing chemical — it keeps rain and insects off

check.explain: Sealing the tank swaps one set of microbes for another, so you get different byproducts and a different cup. The real prize is control: a sealed ferment repeats in a way that open tanks in the sun never will.

items.short: Coffee with roughly 97% of its caffeine removed as green beans, before roasting — almost none, never zero.
items.deep: Decaffeination is a processing step applied to green coffee, months before roasting. Solvent methods use ethyl acetate or methylene chloride; Swiss Water and CO₂ methods use none. All leave a few milligrams per cup — close to nothing, but not nothing.
items.example: A “sugarcane decaf” from Colombia was decaffeinated with ethyl acetate derived from cane.

check.q: Decaffeination happens…

choices.t: In the cup, by brewing shorter

check.explain: It’s a green-coffee processing step — roasting and brewing don’t remove caffeine.

items.short: A solvent-free decaffeination method that pulls caffeine out of green beans with water and a carbon filter.
items.deep: Green beans are soaked in green coffee extract: water already full of everything coffee is made of, except caffeine. Because the water is already loaded with flavour compounds, those stay in the bean, while the caffeine has somewhere to go and leaves. Activated carbon then filters the caffeine out of the water so the same extract can be used again. No solvent ever touches the coffee. Decaf is never caffeine-free, though — US rules set the bar at 97% removed, and Swiss Water reports 99.9%.
items.example: Single origins are usually decaffeinated this way, because origin character survives it best.

sources.label: Barista Magazine — Understanding the Process: Swiss Water Decaffeination

check.q: Why soak the beans in coffee extract instead of plain water?

choices.t: Water would carry flavour out too
Extract dissolves caffeine faster than water
The extract swaps in sugars for the caffeine

check.explain: Every water-based decaf works this way: give a compound nowhere to go and it stays where it is. These methods are judged on what they leave behind, not on what they take out.

items.short: Coffee as it leaves the farm and ships: dried, hulled, unroasted seeds — pale green, hard, and smelling of hay.
items.deep: Everything before the roaster happens to green coffee, and everything after is the roaster’s work on it. Green keeps for months in a sack, which is why it, not roasted coffee, is what gets graded, traded and shipped.
items.example: A roaster buys green coffee by the sack and roasts it in small batches to order.

check.q: Green coffee is…
check.explain: It’s the unroasted seed — what farms sell and roasters buy.

items.short: The shared site where a village’s cherries are pulped, fermented, washed and dried — often the real author of a coffee’s cup.
items.deep: Smallholders rarely process their own cherries. They deliver to a station, which does the work for hundreds of farms at once — so on a Kenyan or Ethiopian bag, the station name is the closest thing to a producer name you get.
items.example: Two Ethiopian lots from the same hillside can taste different because they went to different stations.

items.short: An Indonesian method where the parchment comes off while the bean is still damp — the source of that earthy, heavy Sumatran cup.
items.deep: Elsewhere coffee dries fully inside its parchment; here it is hulled part-dried, at high moisture, and finishes drying bare. It is a response to a wet climate that never gives you enough dry days, and it turns the beans a distinctive jade colour.
items.example: A wet-hulled Sumatra reads as earthy, herbal and cedar-like, with very low acidity.

items.short: The audible pop during roasting when beans expand and steam escapes — the threshold of a drinkable roast.
items.deep: As beans heat, moisture turns to steam and pressure builds until the bean cracks open, like popcorn. First crack marks the start of light-roast territory; how far past it you go decides light, medium, or dark.
items.example: Pulling beans just after first crack gives a bright, light roast.

sources.label: Scott Rao — The Coffee Roaster’s Companion

check.q: First crack signals…

choices.t: The start of a drinkable roast
Second crack is about to begin

check.explain: First crack is the audible milestone where a roast becomes light-roast ready.

items.short: How far a coffee is roasted — light, medium, or dark — which shapes acidity, body and bitterness.
items.deep: Lighter roasts keep more origin character and acidity; darker roasts trade that for body, bitterness and roasty notes. Neither is “better” — it’s a flavour choice.
items.example: A light roast tastes of the bean; a dark roast tastes more of the roast.

check.q: As roast level gets darker, acidity usually…
check.explain: Darker roasting burns off acidity and adds bitterness and body.

items.short: A second, quieter cracking deeper into the roast that marks the edge of dark-roast territory.
items.deep: Deeper into the roast the cell walls break down again. It is quieter and faster than first crack — a crackle rather than a pop — and oils start working their way to the surface of the bean. Past that point you are in dark-roast territory: bittersweet, smoky, low in acidity, tasting more of the roast than of where it grew. Oil on the outside of the bean also turns rancid sooner, which is why dark roasts keep for less time.
items.example: Beans that look glossy in the bag went at least as far as second crack.

sources.label: Scott Rao — The Coffee Roaster’s Companion

check.q: What does a sheen of oil on the beans tell you?

choices.t: The lot was natural, not washed

check.explain: Oil on the surface tells you how far the roast went, not how fresh the beans are or how they were processed. If anything it means the coffee will fade sooner.

items.short: The stretch after first crack that balances the inside and outside of the bean.
items.deep: Development is the time between first crack and the moment the roaster drops the beans, while the heat finishes working through to the middle of each bean. Cut it short and the inside never catches up with the outside: the cup tastes grassy, hollow and drying. That is pale coffee, not bright coffee. Roasters track development as a share of the whole roast rather than as a temperature, because what matters is the proportion.
items.example: Roasters talk about development as a ratio — often around a fifth to a quarter of the whole roast.

sources.label: Scott Rao — The Coffee Roaster’s Companion

check.q: Brewed to a recipe you trust, a light roast still tastes grassy and hollow. What is the fault?

choices.t: Dropped too soon after first crack
Taken too dark for its origin
A blend rather than a single origin

check.explain: The colour tells you where the roast stopped. Development tells you whether the middle of the bean caught up. People mix up “light” and “underdeveloped” all the time, and only one of the two is a fault.

items.short: When the coffee was roasted — fresher is better; aim to brew within a few weeks.
items.deep: The roast date is the only date on a bag that measures anything. A best-before date is chosen by whoever packed the coffee, often a year ahead, and tells you nothing about when it was roasted. Whole beans are usually at their best from a few days after roasting, once the worst of the degassing is over, until a few weeks after. A bag with no roast date on it is telling you something too.
items.example: “Roasted 9 days ago” is a fact; “best before March 2027” is a shelf-life promise.

sources.label: National Coffee Association — Storage and shelf life

check.q: One bag is best-before in eight months; another was roasted eleven days ago. Which is the better bet?

choices.t: The dated one — you know where it sits in its life
The best-before one, which guarantees eight months of freshness
Neither matters as long as the beans are whole

check.explain: Freshness is really the distance from the roast, and only a roast date measures that. Keeping the beans whole slows the decline, but it does not reset the clock.

items.short: Roasted beans releasing built-up CO₂ for days after roasting — the gas behind the bloom.
items.deep: Roasting traps carbon dioxide inside the bean, and it leaks out for days or weeks afterwards — fastest in the first few days, and much faster once the coffee is ground. Brew too early and the escaping gas stops the water soaking the grounds evenly. Wait too long and the aromas have drifted off along with it. Filter coffee usually wants a few days of rest; espresso wants rather more.
items.example: Espresso pulled the day after roasting gushes crema and tastes thin — the gas is in the way.

sources.label: Food Research International — Roasting conditions and CO₂ degassing behaviour
J. Agric. Food Chem. — Time-resolved gravimetric assessment of coffee degassing

check.q: Why does very fresh coffee often brew unevenly?

choices.t: Fresh beans are harder, so grind coarser
The oils have not yet reached the surface

check.explain: The bloom is that gas escaping where you can see it. Resting the coffee gives up a little aroma in exchange for an even extraction. Espresso gets the longer rest because the water only has seconds to do its work, not minutes.

items.short: Carbon dioxide — the gas roasting traps inside the bean, and the reason fresh grounds bloom.
items.deep: Roasting generates carbon dioxide and locks it in the bean, which then leaks out for days or weeks afterwards. That escaping gas is what makes fresh grounds swell in the bloom, what fills the valve on a bag, and part of what builds crema on an espresso shot. As it leaves, oxygen and moisture take its place — which is staling.
items.example: A bag with a one-way valve is letting CO₂ out without letting air in.

check.q: A flat bloom on fresh-looking grounds usually means…
check.explain: No bloom means no trapped CO₂ left — the coffee was roasted or ground too long ago.

items.short: Flavour fading as oxygen gets at the coffee — slow for whole beans, fast once ground.
items.deep: Staling is oxidation, not gas escaping: oxygen reacts with the oils and aromas in the coffee, and heat, light and damp all speed that up. Whole beans hold on for weeks. Ground coffee fades within days, because grinding exposes far more surface to the air. Stale coffee tastes papery, woody and flat.
items.example: Grinding a week’s worth on Sunday costs more flavour than buying cheaper beans would.

sources.label: National Coffee Association — Storage and shelf life

check.q: You can change one thing about how you store coffee. Which does the most?

choices.t: Move the bag into the fridge
Decant into a clear jar on the counter

check.explain: Exposed surface is what drives staling, so grinding at the last minute does more than anything else you can change. The fridge adds moisture and a clear jar lets light in, and both speed up the same reaction.

items.short: The first splash of water on fresh grounds, which releases trapped CO₂ and makes the bed swell and bubble.
items.deep: Fresh coffee is full of carbon dioxide. Wetting it for 30–45 seconds before the main pour lets that gas escape, so water can extract evenly instead of channelling around bubbles.
items.example: A vigorous bloom is a good sign your coffee is fresh.

check.q: The bloom releases…
check.explain: Blooming lets built-up CO₂ escape so extraction is even.

items.short: The proportion of coffee to water — the single biggest lever on strength, often written like 1:16.
items.deep: A 1:16 ratio means 1 gram of coffee to 16 grams of water. Lower numbers (1:12) brew stronger; higher (1:18) brew lighter. Dial this to taste before fiddling with anything else.
items.example: 60 g of coffee to 1,000 g of water is a classic ~1:16 batch-brew ratio.

check.q: A 1:12 ratio versus 1:18 will taste…
check.explain: Less water per gram of coffee (1:12) makes a stronger, more concentrated cup.

items.short: How much flavour is dissolved out of the grounds — too little tastes sour, too much tastes bitter.
items.deep: Water pulls compounds out of coffee in an order: fruity acids first, sweetness next, bitter and dry notes last. The sweet spot — “even extraction” — is the goal of grinding, ratio and time.
items.example: Sour, weak coffee is usually under-extracted; harsh, dry coffee is over-extracted.

check.q: A sour, thin cup is most likely…
check.explain: Sourness usually means too little was extracted — grind finer or brew longer.

items.short: Total Dissolved Solids — the measured number for how strong a brew is, read as a percentage.
items.deep: TDS is the share of the cup that is dissolved coffee rather than water, measured with a refractometer. Filter coffee usually lands between 1.15% and 1.45%; espresso runs far higher, around 8–12%. It answers “how strong”, not “how well extracted” — the same TDS can come from a good ratio or from over-extracting too little coffee, which is why it is always read alongside the brew ratio.
items.example: A cup at 1.20% TDS is weaker than one at 1.40% — but neither number tells you whether it tastes good.

check.q: TDS measures…
check.explain: It is the percentage of dissolved coffee in the cup — strength. Extraction and taste are separate questions.

items.short: Brewing by pouring hot water through grounds in a filter cone, like a V60 or Chemex.
items.deep: Water passes through the bed of grounds once and drains away — nothing sits and steeps. That means the contact time is a result of your grind and how fast you pour, rather than a number you choose. It is the control people love pour-over for, and the reason it is easy to get wrong. Paper holds back most of the oils and fine particles, so the cup tastes clean and light.
items.example: Same coffee, same ratio: a slower pour and a finer grind taste noticeably stronger.

check.q: What makes pour-over harder to repeat than a French press?

choices.t: You set the flow, so time varies
The water has to be hotter

check.explain: With a press, the time is fixed: four minutes is four minutes. With a pour-over the time is an outcome of your own choices, which gives you more control and more to keep steady.

items.short: Brewing by steeping grounds fully in water, like a French press, then separating them.
items.deep: The grounds sit in the full volume of water for a set time, then get separated out — plunged, filtered or poured off. Because the clock is doing the work, immersion is forgiving of an uneven grind: the bigger particles have the whole steep to catch up with the small ones. A metal mesh lets oils and fine particles through, and that is where the heavier body comes from.
items.example: Cold brew and a French press are the same idea run at different temperatures.

check.q: Which method is kindest to someone without a good grinder?

choices.t: Pour-over, if you pour more slowly

check.explain: Particles of different sizes extract at different speeds. A long steep closes that gap; pressure widens it. Espresso is the harshest test of a grinder there is.

items.short: Coffee steeped in cold water for 12–24 hours instead of brewed hot — smooth, low-acid, and strong.
items.deep: Cold water pulls out sugars and caffeine but leaves most of the bright acids and bitter compounds behind, which is why it tastes round and chocolatey. It is usually brewed as a concentrate and diluted, so a serving carries more caffeine than a mug of drip.
items.example: A 1:8 concentrate steeped overnight, then cut with water or milk to taste.

items.short: A small, concentrated coffee pulled by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee under about 9 bars of pressure.
items.deep: Not a roast level and not a bean — a brewing method. Pressure does in 25–30 seconds what a filter brew takes minutes to do, giving a syrupy cup several times stronger than drip, topped with crema. Everything milk drinks are built on starts here.
items.example: A typical modern shot: 18 g of coffee in, ~36 g of liquid out, in about 28 seconds.

check.q: Espresso is defined by…
check.explain: It’s a brewing method — pressure through finely ground coffee — not a roast or a bean.

items.short: Adjusting the grind until a shot runs in the time you want and tastes right — the daily ritual of espresso.
items.deep: You hold the dose and the target output steady and move only the grind: finer slows the shot and pushes extraction up, coarser speeds it up. Fresh coffee, humidity and the bag’s age all shift it, so yesterday’s setting rarely survives today.
items.example: The shot ran in 18 seconds and tasted sour, so you grind finer and pull again.

items.short: The reddish-brown foam on top of an espresso shot, made of emulsified oils and CO₂.
items.deep: Crema forms when pressurised water forces oils and gases into a fine emulsion. It’s a sign of fresh coffee and a well-pulled shot, though it isn’t the whole story of quality.
items.example: A thick, hazelnut-coloured crema usually means fresh beans and a good extraction.

check.q: Crema is mostly made of…
check.explain: Crema is an emulsion of coffee oils and dissolved gas, not milk.

items.short: The handled basket that holds the coffee grounds and locks into an espresso machine.
items.deep: You grind into the portafilter, distribute and tamp the grounds level, then lock it into the group head. Even, well-tamped coffee in the basket is the key to an even shot.
items.example: Knocking the spent puck out of the portafilter is the satisfying clack you hear in cafés.

check.q: The portafilter…

choices.t: Holds the grounds and locks into the machine

check.explain: It’s the basket-and-handle that carries the tamped coffee into the group head.

items.short: An espresso “cut” with a small, equal amount of warm milk to soften it.
items.deep: Cortado means “cut”: a shot cut with roughly its own volume of warm steamed milk, and hardly any foam. The ratio is the whole point — enough milk to take the edge off the acidity and bitterness, not enough to bury the coffee. That ratio is also the main thing separating one café milk drink from another.
items.example: A cortado runs about 1:1 espresso to milk; a latte can be 1:5 or looser.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: What separates a cortado from a latte?

choices.t: The milk is warmed but never steamed
It is pulled as a longer, weaker shot

check.explain: Milk drinks mostly differ in one way: how much milk goes in per shot. The names are ratios, not different kinds of coffee.

items.short: When water forces a path through cracks in the espresso puck, extracting unevenly.
items.deep: Water takes the easiest route through the coffee, floods it, and leaves the rest of the bed barely brewed — which is how one shot manages to taste sour and bitter at the same time. The causes are all in the puck rather than the machine: clumps, cracks, grounds spread unevenly, or a tamp that went in at an angle. Look at the spent puck afterwards and you will see streaks or small craters.
items.example: Sour and harsh in the same sip is the signature; a shot that merely ran fast is a different problem.

check.q: A shot tastes sour and bitter at the same time. What does that point to?

choices.t: A grind that is simply too fine

check.explain: A mistake that affects the whole puck evenly pushes the cup one way or the other. Two opposite faults at once mean parts of the bed brewed and parts did not — that is how you prepared it, not where the grinder is set.

items.short: Pressing the espresso grounds flat and firm in the portafilter for an even shot.
items.deep: Tamping presses the grounds into a level bed so the water meets the same resistance everywhere. Level matters more than hard: once the press is firm and even, pushing harder changes very little, while a tamp that sits a degree or two off level sends water down one side. It also cannot fix badly spread grounds — clumps pressed flat are still clumps.
items.example: Baristas practise tamping level rather than hard; the puck should end up like a polished floor.

check.q: Which does more for a shot — tamping harder, or tamping level?

choices.t: Harder — tamp pressure sets the shot time
Neither, once the basket is full to the rim

check.explain: How much resistance the puck gives comes mostly from the grind and the dose. How even it is comes from your hands. Water goes wherever the bed is weakest, so a flat tamp is the part worth practising.

items.short: The bright, tangy liveliness in coffee — pleasant acidity tastes crisp, like citrus or apple, not sour.
items.deep: Acidity is a positive quality in tasting language, distinct from “sour” (a fault of under-extraction). High-grown washed coffees tend to be the most acidic, in a sparkling, mouth-watering way.
items.example: A Kenyan’s juicy, blackcurrant acidity is what fans love about it.

check.q: In tasting terms, pleasant acidity is…
check.explain: Acidity is prized brightness — different from the sour taste of under-extraction.

items.short: How heavy or full a coffee feels in your mouth — from tea-like and light to syrupy and thick.
items.deep: Also called mouthfeel. Body comes from oils and fine particles suspended in the brew. A French press feels heavier than a paper-filtered pour-over because the filter holds less back.
items.example: Naturals and dark roasts often feel fuller-bodied.

check.q: Body refers to…

choices.t: The coffee’s weight and texture in the mouth

check.explain: Body is the tactile weight of the cup — light and tea-like to thick and syrupy.

items.short: The texture and weight of coffee on your tongue — another word for body.
items.deep: Mouthfeel is what you feel rather than what you taste: the weight, the texture, how thick the coffee is. It comes from dissolved solids plus whatever oils and fine particles are still floating in the cup, so the filter you brew through changes it more than the coffee itself does. Cuppers score it in its own section, separate from flavour.
items.example: The same coffee is silkier from a press than through paper — same beans, same ratio.

sources.label: SCA — Evolving the cupping protocol and form

check.q: Where does a French press get its heavier mouthfeel?

choices.t: Oils and fines through the mesh
A larger dose of coffee per cup

check.explain: Texture and strength are two different things. Swap paper for a metal mesh and the body changes even though the recipe has not. It is the cheapest experiment in brewing.

items.short: The flavour that lingers after you swallow — short and clean, or long and sweet.
items.deep: The finish — cuppers call it aftertaste — is what is left once you have swallowed: how long it lasts, and whether it stays pleasant. Good coffee fades away sweet and clean. Tired or badly brewed coffee turns papery, drying or ashy a few seconds later. It gets its own score because a cup can taste lovely at first and then fall apart.
items.example: Wait ten seconds after swallowing before judging it — the finish arrives late by definition.

sources.label: SCA — Evolving the cupping protocol and form

check.q: A cup tastes fine, then turns dry and papery ten seconds later. What have you learned?
check.explain: Different faults show up at different points in a sip, which is why the first taste and the finish are scored separately. Papery and woody are the words for stale coffee; astringent and ashy point at a brewing problem instead.

items.short: How well a coffee’s sweetness, acidity, body and bitterness fit together.
items.deep: Balance asks whether the parts fit together — acidity, sweetness, body, bitterness, finish — not whether any one of them is quiet. A powerful coffee can be balanced, and a dull one can be unbalanced. Cuppers score it after the individual qualities, because it is a judgement about how those relate to each other.
items.example: A searing Kenyan acidity carried by enough sweetness scores well; the same acidity alone does not.

sources.label: SCA — Evolving the cupping protocol and form

check.q: Which is better balanced — a fierce, very acidic Kenyan whose sweetness carries it, or a mild cup with nothing sticking out?

choices.t: The mild one; nothing dominates it

check.explain: Balance is about how the parts relate, so a cup with very little in it has very little to balance. Strength and harmony are separate judgements: plenty of bold coffees are perfectly harmonious.

items.short: The industry’s standard tasting method: same grind, same water, no filter — slurped from a spoon and scored.
items.deep: Grounds steep in a bowl, the crust is broken, and tasters slurp across many bowls side by side. Holding every variable but the coffee still lets buyers compare lots fairly, and the 100-point score that comes out of it is what puts a coffee above the specialty line.
items.example: A lot cupping at 86 points will be sold as specialty; one at 78 goes to commodity blends.

items.short: A grinder that crushes beans between two burrs for an even, adjustable grind — the single best brewing upgrade.
items.deep: Unlike blade grinders that chop randomly, burrs produce uniform particles, which is essential for even extraction. The gap between the burrs sets how fine or coarse you grind.
items.example: Switching from a blade to a burr grinder is the upgrade most people notice first.

check.q: Burr grinders are better because they…
check.explain: Even particle size from burrs gives more even, better-tasting extraction.

items.short: A kettle with a long, curved spout that gives slow, precise control over your pour.
items.deep: The narrow spout lets you place water exactly where you want it and control the flow rate — important for even pour-over brewing and a controlled bloom.
items.example: A gooseneck makes it easy to pour in slow, steady spirals over the grounds.

check.q: A gooseneck kettle helps you…
check.explain: Its curved spout is all about pour control, not speed.

items.short: A compact plunger brewer that uses gentle pressure to make a quick, clean cup.
items.deep: A chamber, a paper or metal filter, and a plunger. The coffee steeps for a short time, then you press it through in seconds. As it comes out of the box that press is gentle — around a bar, against the nine or so a machine uses for espresso — so it mostly speeds up the drain, and what you get is a short, clean immersion brew. Add-on caps with a pressure valve change that: they hold the brew back until the pressure builds, and a fine grind and tight ratio then give you a concentrated, foam-topped shot much closer to espresso. It travels well and is forgiving about grind, which is most of the reason people love it.
items.example: Two minutes of steep and a slow twenty-second press is a good default recipe.

check.q: Two people brew the same beans in an AeroPress, one with a valve cap fitted. Why is only one cup espresso-like?

choices.t: The valve holds pressure back until it builds
The valve raises the brewing temperature
The valve doses more coffee into the chamber

check.explain: A plain AeroPress lets water through as you push, so pressure never gets a chance to build and the result behaves like filter coffee. A valve makes the brew wait, and pressure is what pulls out the concentration and foam people recognise as espresso.

items.short: An hourglass-shaped pour-over brewer using thick filters for an exceptionally clean cup.
items.deep: An hourglass of heatproof glass with a thick, folded paper filter. That paper is heavier than most, so it holds back more oil and fine particles and slows the drain down as it does. The cup comes out unusually clean and tea-like, and the thick paper is why Chemex recipes ask for a coarser grind than a V60 at the same dose.
items.example: Grind a notch coarser than you would for a V60, or the brew stalls in the paper.

check.q: Why do Chemex recipes ask for a coarser grind than a V60?

choices.t: It holds more water at once

check.explain: The grind has to suit how fast the brewer drains. Thick paper already slows the flow, so a fine grind on top of that stalls the bed and over-extracts whatever does get through. The same paper does two things at once: it slows the drain and it cleans up the cup.

items.short: A cone-shaped pour-over dripper with a 60° angle and spiral ribs — the default filter brewer in most cafés.
items.deep: Made by Hario. The single large hole means you, not the cone, control the flow: pour rate and grind size decide the brew time. It rewards a medium grind and a steady pour, and it is the brewer most recipes online are written for.
items.example: Most pour-over recipes you find assume a V60 unless they say otherwise.

items.short: A steeping jug with a mesh plunger — grounds sit in the water the whole time, giving a heavy, full-bodied cup.
items.deep: The simplest good brewer there is: coarse grind, four minutes, press slowly. Metal mesh lets oils and fine particles through where paper would trap them, which is exactly why it feels thicker than a pour-over.
items.example: Coarse grind, 1:15, four minutes, then press and pour it all out so it stops brewing.

items.short: A small kitchen scale lets you weigh coffee and water for a repeatable brew ratio.
items.deep: Coffee is measured by weight because volume is unreliable: a scoop of light roast weighs more than the same scoop of a dark one, and the grind size changes how much fits in the spoon. A scale that reads to 0.1 g, ideally with a timer, turns a recipe into something you can repeat — the same ratio every morning, so when the cup changes you know it was because of something you changed. Rules of thumb like tablespoons per cup are a starting point, not a recipe.
items.example: 60 g of coffee to 1,000 g of water is a recipe; “two scoops” is a guess.

check.q: Why do baristas weigh rather than scoop?

choices.t: Scales read the water temperature too
Coffee absorbs water differently by volume

check.explain: A brew ratio compares two weights, so measuring by the scoop quietly changes it every time you switch beans. Weighing is what lets you compare yesterday’s brew to today’s.

items.short: How coarse or fine the coffee is ground — the main dial for matching your brew method.
items.deep: The grind decides how much coffee surface the water can reach, which makes it the fastest way to change how quickly a brew extracts: finer is quicker, coarser is slower. Each method comes with its own contact time — seconds for espresso, minutes for a press, hours for cold brew — so the method sets the rough range and your taste decides where in that range you land. How even the grind is matters as much as how fine, and that is the whole argument for burr grinders over blades.
items.example: Espresso runs near table salt; a French press nearer coarse sea salt.

check.q: You brew a pour-over with the grind you use for a French press. What happens?

choices.t: Nothing: grind and method are independent

check.explain: Grind and contact time work against each other, so changing the method means changing the grind. A coarse grind in a fast brewer tastes sour and thin no matter how good the coffee is.

items.short: The dust-sized particles every grinder produces alongside the grind you asked for — they over-extract and can clog the filter.
items.deep: No grinder is perfectly even; there is always a tail of powder. Fines give up their flavour fastest, so too many read as bitter and dry, and they slow a brew by packing into the filter bed. Better burrs make fewer of them; sifting or a slightly coarser grind manages the rest.
items.example: A brew that stalls and tastes harsh is often drowning in fines from a worn grinder.

items.short: Coffee from one place — a country, region, or even a single farm — rather than a blend.
items.deep: Single origins let you taste the character of a specific place and harvest. Blends mix origins for consistency or a target flavour; single origins celebrate difference.
items.example: “Ethiopia Yirgacheffe” is a single origin; “House Blend” usually isn’t.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: A single-origin coffee comes from…
check.explain: Single origin means one source — country, region or farm — not a blend.

items.short: A certification that guarantees farmers a minimum price and community premiums for their coffee.
items.deep: Fair Trade sets a price floor to protect growers from volatile markets and adds a premium for community projects. It’s one of several models aiming to make the supply chain fairer.
items.example: A Fair Trade label means the co-op was paid at least the guaranteed minimum.

check.q: Fair Trade mainly guarantees…
check.explain: Its core promise is a price floor plus a community premium for growers.

items.short: Roasters buying straight from farmers, often paying above market for quality and relationships.
items.deep: Direct trade is a roaster describing how they buy: straight from the producer or through a single exporter, usually paying above the market rate, often from the same farms year after year. Nobody audits the phrase, so by itself it guarantees nothing. What makes it checkable is the detail a roaster publishes — the price they paid, the names of the farms and lots, how many years they have been buying there. Certification works the other way round: it is audited, but it usually sets a floor rather than a premium.
items.example: A transparency report listing the price paid per kilo turns the claim into something you can check.

check.q: What does “direct trade” on a bag guarantee?

choices.t: A minimum price set by a certifier
That the roaster visited the farm

check.explain: The label tells you what the roaster intends. The evidence is whatever they publish alongside it. Certification is the opposite trade-off: someone checks it, but what it guarantees is a minimum price, not a good one.

items.short: Knowing exactly where a coffee came from, down to the farm or washing station.
items.deep: Traceability is how far back a coffee can be followed: to a country, a region, a washing station or co-op, a farm, sometimes even a single day’s picking. Following it further back does not automatically mean it tastes better — what it buys you is quality that can be repeated and a premium you can check. Commodity coffee is traceable to a country and a grade, so a bag that says only “Brazil” is telling you where the trail runs out.
items.example: “Ethiopia” is an origin; “Gedeb, Worka Sakaro, lot 12” is traceability.

sources.label: James Hoffmann — The World Atlas of Coffee

check.q: A bag names the washing station but no farm. Is that a traceability failure?

choices.t: No — the station is the real unit
Yes; only a farm name counts
Yes, unless the roaster is certified

check.explain: What matters is naming the place where the lot was actually made. In much of East Africa hundreds of small farms deliver their cherries to one washing station, and the lot is created there — so the station is the honest answer. Demanding a single farm name would only encourage roasters to make one up.

items.short: The Specialty Coffee Association — the trade body behind the standards, flavour wheel and scoring most of this app leans on.
items.deep: A non-profit of producers, roasters, baristas and buyers. It publishes the brewing and water standards, the 100-point cupping scale, the barista and brewing certifications, and the Coffee Taster’s Flavor Wheel. When a bag or a café cites a score or a “standard”, this is usually whose.
items.example: The flavour wheel in this app is built on the SCA lexicon.

check.q: The SCA is…

choices.t: A coffee trade body that publishes standards

check.explain: It is the Specialty Coffee Association — the industry body behind the standards and the flavour wheel.

items.short: The national bodies that regulate, promote and count each origin’s coffee — the source behind most origin statistics.
items.deep: Almost every producing country has one: CECAFÉ and CONAB in Brazil, Anacafé in Guatemala, ICAFE in Costa Rica, IHCAFE in Honduras, NAEB in Rwanda, the Coffee Board of India, VICOFA in Vietnam. They set regional maps and quality rules, publish harvest and export figures, and are who the Atlas cites for crop numbers.
items.example: Anacafé drew the eight-region map of Guatemala that buyers still use.

sources.label: National coffee institutes — published crop and export data

items.short: High-quality coffee scoring 80+ points on a 100-point scale, made with care at every step.
items.deep: In the trade, specialty is a threshold rather than a style: green coffee that stays inside a defect limit and scores 80 or more on the 100-point cupping form. In everyday use the word also describes a supply chain that pays for quality and can tell you where the coffee came from. It does not mean expensive, single-origin or dark — blends clear 80 all the time.
items.example: On a green-coffee invoice, “specialty grade” means inside the defect limit and 80+ on the form.

sources.label: SCA — Evolving the cupping protocol and form

check.q: What makes a coffee “specialty” in the trade sense?

choices.t: A retail price above a set threshold

check.explain: It is a tasting score with a defect count behind it. That is why a blend can be specialty while an expensive single origin falls short.
